name: Eyelid pulling

lead: Eyelid pulling is a looksmaxxing practice in which people pull or stretch the upper eyelid skin by hand, usually in front of a mirror, hoping the skin will sit lower or looser over time. The goal is to reduce upper eyelid exposure, the amount of eyelid visible between lashes and brow, and to look more hooded.

Participants on looksmax.org post before and after photos and report temporary or lasting changes, while others in the same threads say the effect is just a change from how the lid sits. No clinical study has examined the routine for appearance.

paras: Practitioners describe pulling or tucking the lid with a finger for a few minutes a day, often followed by moisturiser, and sometimes combined with cold exposure or topical products meant to plump the area. Forum threads debate where to pull and for how long; reports of results range from a day to over a year.

No trials describe safety for this routine. Delicate eyelid skin can become irritated or asymmetrical with repeated manipulation, and one forum poster reported creating an asymmetry on the first day. Clinicians treat eyelid changes such as sagging or retraction with medical or surgical assessment, not with a home routine.

angle.text: Practitioners aim to lower the position of the upper eyelid fold so less lid shows between lashes and brow. The change they describe is in the lid's resting position and is reported as partly temporary, with some expecting it to build with repeated sessions.

lead: Eyelid pulling is a practice from looksmaxxing forums in which a person manually pulls or tucks the upper eyelid skin to change how much of the lid is visible. The stated aim is to reduce upper eyelid exposure (UEE), the visible stretch of eyelid between lashline and brow, and to produce more hooded eyes, a look many in these communities prize. [1][2]

Participants describe it as a free, non-surgical way to alter eye area appearance. Some pair it with cold treatments and topical products meant to change the skin of the lid and brow region. Results are shared as before and after photos, and threads regularly ask about technique, duration and whether the effect lasts. [1][2][3]

No published research has tested deliberate eyelid pulling for appearance. The medical literature that uses similar words concerns other topics: a 1990 case series described children who pulled their eyelids as a habit, and clinical reviews describe eyelid margin conditions such as ectropion. [4][5]

paras: Upper eyelid exposure is the amount of upper lid skin visible when the eyes are open and looking forward. People with high exposure sometimes wish for the less visible lid associated with hooded eyes. Eyelid pulling is one of several do-it-yourself approaches used to try to lower that exposure without surgery. [1][2]

Threads describe sessions of pulling on parts of the lid, with disagreement over which section to target and whether to pull upward, outward or toward the nose. Users commonly follow with moisturiser and some report combining it with cold applications and plumping topicals to the lid and brow-bone area. [2][3]

Reports of results differ. One poster described fast visible changes that partly receded during the day but did not return fully to baseline, and expected the changes eventually to become close to permanent. [2] Others in the same communities answered that the effect is temporary or posted skeptical replies. [3][6]

No clinical study has examined eyelid pulling as an appearance technique. A 1990 report of five children aged 3 to 9 who pulled on their eyelids found the habit resolved within about two weeks with reassurance alone, which concerns a behaviour rather than a cosmetic technique. [4]

Ophthalmology literature describes ectropion, the outward turning of the eyelid margin, as arising from laxity of the canthal tendons, scarring, facial nerve paralysis or mechanical causes. [5] No study links deliberate eyelid pulling to these conditions.

Participants have reported unintended asymmetry from early sessions, and eyelid skin is thin and delicate. Because the practice is untested, its effects on the lid over time are undocumented. Eyelid ptosis, laxity or retraction are medical matters for an eye specialist. [2][5]
